items.question: What sets Cyrrus apart from a traditional strategy consultancy?
items.answer: Three things. The same team that runs the diagnosis stays for execution, instead of handing over a report and leaving. We start implementing from week 1, not at the end of the diagnosis. And we're vendor-agnostic, so the strategy doesn't end up recommending the technology someone wants to sell. Results are measured in business indicators, not in the page count of the report.

items.question: When should a company hire a strategic planning consultant?
items.answer: A company needs strategic consulting when plans exist but aren't executed consistently across areas, when financial indicators take weeks to become available for decision-making, or when business growth depends too heavily on the constant presence of the founder or leadership team. It's also the right moment when a mid-size or large corporation needs business transformation, IT strategy, or business continuity in the face of a change in market, technology, or organizational structure, and requires an external partner to help execute — not just diagnose.

items.question: What does IT strategy consulting include?
items.answer: Aligning technology with the business: a target architecture and a portfolio of initiatives (ERP, CRM, data, AI) prioritized by impact, each with its business case, plus the criteria against which any later technology decision will be evaluated. Because Cyrrus is vendor-agnostic, the strategy doesn't end up recommending the technology someone wants to sell.

items.question: How long does a strategic planning process take?
items.answer: As a reference, the Build phase of the CIRA method takes 4 to 8 weeks, depending on organization size and how many areas are involved, and covers the diagnostic, the roadmap, and its prioritization by impact.

items.question: What is the difference between a CTO as a Service and hiring a full-time CTO?
items.answer: A CTO as a Service gives you access to the judgment and the experience without the fixed cost of a full-time executive, and it is the right figure when a company needs senior technology direction but does not have the daily decision volume to justify the role. The practical difference is dedication, not depth of judgment.

items.question: What deliverables does a strategy engagement with Cyrrus produce?
items.answer: A diagnostic of the current state of processes and technology, a roadmap prioritized by business impact over a defined horizon, the business case for the highest-weight initiatives, and the criteria against which any later technology decision will be evaluated.

items.answer: Those are the following phases of the CIRA Method. Once the roadmap defines what needs to be solved, Identify selects the technology (ERP, CRM, or other), Realize manages the implementation project, and Adopt makes sure the organization actually uses it. You can hire just the strategic diagnosis or the full engagement.

body: An IT strategy answers a simple question: what technology does the company need to execute its business strategy, and in what order. Without that answer, every department buys its own tool, systems don't integrate, and the technology budget is decided project by project.

That is why an IT strategy doesn't start with technology but with the business: what the company wants to achieve in the coming years, which processes sustain it, and where current technology holds it back. With that diagnosis we define the target architecture and the portfolio of initiatives.

Each initiative in the portfolio carries its business case: expected benefit, multi-year total cost (not just the license), risk and owner. That is what lets leadership approve, postpone or discard with the same criteria, and what is later used to measure whether the investment delivered.

In our view, the costliest mistakes in an IT strategy are choosing software before defining the architecture, planning without an owner per initiative, and not reviewing the portfolio when the business changes. IT governance — who decides and with which indicators — is what prevents all three.

This service is part of the Construct phase of the CIRA method. From here come the criteria we use to select software and infrastructure with no vendor bias (Identify phase), the plan that Project Management governs (Realize), and the foundation of change management (Adopt). It can also be engaged as CIO or CTO as a Service, when the company needs technology leadership without a full-time executive.

respuesta.title: What does business continuity consulting do?
respuesta.body: It defines how the company keeps operating when something critical fails. It starts from a business impact analysis (BIA) that identifies which processes are indispensable and how much damage each hour without them causes; from there come the recovery targets (RTO and RPO), the business continuity plan (BCP) and the disaster recovery plan (DRP). The plan belongs to leadership, not only to the IT department.

body: A business continuity plan defines how the organization keeps operating when something critical fails: a system, a supplier, a site or a key person. It is not an IT document: it is a leadership decision about which processes cannot stop and how much the company is willing to invest so they don't.

That is why we start with the business impact analysis (BIA). According to NIST SP 800-34, the BIA correlates each system with the business processes it supports and, based on that, characterizes the consequences of a disruption. From there come two measurable targets: the RTO, the maximum time a resource can remain unavailable before there is an unacceptable impact, and the RPO, the point in time to which data can be recovered after an outage.

With the targets defined, the continuity strategies and the disaster recovery plan (DRP) are designed: which systems are restored, in what order, with which backups and who decides. The same guide distinguishes the business continuity plan (BCP), focused on sustaining business processes during and after a disruption, from the DRP, focused on restoring information systems.

In our view, the most frequent mistake is having a plan that has never been tested. A drill with a real scenario — the ERP goes down on a Monday at 9 a.m. — shows in hours what a document doesn't show in months: who didn't know they had to decide, which backup didn't restore, and which vendor didn't answer.

ISO 22301:2019 is the international reference for business continuity management systems: a framework to plan, implement, operate, review and improve a documented management system that protects the organization from disruptive incidents and ensures recovery. Not every company needs to certify, but every company needs a plan that holds up to that logic. If the plan requires new backup, high-availability or alternate-site solutions, we select them with our infrastructure consulting, with no vendor commissions, and Project Management governs the implementation.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions about business continuity consulting

items.question: When should a company hire business continuity consulting services?
items.answer: When the operation depends on one or two systems and no one has tested what happens if they go down; when a customer, a bank or a regulator asks for the continuity plan; when the company migrated critical infrastructure to the cloud and the old plan no longer applies; or when a plan exists on paper but has never been rehearsed.

items.question: What is the difference between a business continuity plan (BCP), a disaster recovery plan (DRP) and a contingency plan?
items.answer: According to NIST SP 800-34, the business continuity plan focuses on sustaining business processes during and after a disruption; the DRP is an information-system-focused plan to restore systems, usually at an alternate site, after a major disruption; and a system's contingency plan describes how to assess and recover that specific system. The BCP belongs to leadership; the DRP and contingency plans to IT; all three must be coordinated.

items.question: What is the BIA and what results does it leave?
items.answer: The business impact analysis correlates each system with the processes it supports and characterizes the consequences of a disruption. It leaves three results: which processes are critical and how long they tolerate being down, which resources are needed to recover them, and in what order they are recovered.

items.question: What are the RTO and the RPO?
items.answer: The RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum time a resource can remain unavailable before causing an unacceptable impact on the processes it supports. The RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the point in time, prior to the outage, to which data can be recovered with the latest backup; it measures how much data loss the process tolerates. Leadership sets them with the business, not the vendor.

items.question: Do we need ISO 22301 certification?
items.answer: It is not mandatory. ISO 22301:2019 is the international standard for business continuity management systems and serves as a reference to structure the plan; certifying makes sense when a customer or the sector requires it. Our service defines and tests the plan; if the company decides to certify, the plan is built with that logic.

items.question: Who implements the solutions the plan requires?
items.answer: If the plan requires backup, high availability, an alternate site or cloud, we select the solutions with our infrastructure consulting, with no vendor commissions, and Project Management (PMO) governs the implementation.

items.question: How long does the commercial action plan take?
items.answer: The initial work and delivery take about 8 weeks. After that, execution is up to the company and a review is included three months after delivery.

items.question: Which commercial decisions are made?
items.answer: Seven: growth priority, market, priority customer (ICP), situation and need, value and differentiation, offer and access to market.

items.question: Who carries out the plan?
items.answer: The company: you make the decisions and execute. The roadmap defines what to change, what comes first, who owns it and what to watch.

items.question: What does the three-month review include?
items.answer: An adoption review and commercial recalibration, included in the service: what was implemented, what changed and what should be adjusted, with recommendations and an updated roadmap.

items.question: Why does it include an AI positioning study?
items.answer: Because buyers already use AI when they buy: according to a Gartner survey of 646 B2B buyers (August–September 2025), 45% used AI tools during a recent purchase. The study reviews how AI finds, describes and evaluates you.

items.question: How does it start?
items.answer: With a conversation about what could happen if you stay as you are and what change would make it worthwhile. If there is a fit, we define the scope and the proposal.
